name: Sequoia National Park
blurb: Giant sequoia groves above oak foothills, fed by the Kaweah and the Sierra snow.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Fire dries and opens sequoia cones and clears rival growth. Set Fire to -100% and watch the sequoia, then the cone-eaters that depend on it.

sources.title: NPS: Mammals and birds of Sequoia and Kings Canyon

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Sequoia National Park, Sequoiadendron giganteum, Acorn woodpecker). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Hot, dry foothill summers and cool, snowy mountain winters set the growing season from oak woodland up to the sequoia groves.
Giant sequoias are adapted to fire, which dries cones, clears rival growth and exposes bare soil. Fire suppression let fuel build up, and large recent fires burned in the groves.
Foothill and forest soils hold the nutrients that oaks, shrubs and sequoias draw up, replenished by fallen leaves, wood and droppings.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen needles, acorn husks, wood and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
The most massive single-stem tree on Earth, growing in groves such as Giant Forest at roughly 5,500 to 9,000 feet. Its cones open mainly through fire heat and insect damage.
Links the foothill chaparral to the higher conifer forest. Its acorns are a food for deer, bears and woodpeckers.
Strips scales off cones for the seeds and eats giant sequoia cone scales, acorns and mushrooms. Discarded scales pile up in middens.
Mostly browses shrubs and trees, with forbs, fruit and acorns, from the foothills to the montane forest. Main large prey of mountain lions.
The most-recorded bumble bee near the park. Forages on a range of wildflowers and shrubs and nests underground, often in rodent burrows.
Eats mostly land invertebrates, mainly insects, and is an important food for snakes and birds of prey.
Eats small mammals, birds and reptiles; Californian snakes take more lizards than elsewhere.
The most-recorded bird near the park, an opportunistic feeder that scavenges carrion.
Soars over the foothills looking for carrion.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: Omnivore: mostly plants and acorns, plus insects such as bees and ants, carrion, and in spring deer fawns.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: Prefers deer among large prey and takes smaller animals too. In California black bears visit many of its kills.
A soaring hawk of the foothills; GloBI records show it eating lizards, rattlesnakes, ravens and woodpeckers near the park.

story: Sequoia National Park in California protects 404,064 acres in the southern Sierra Nevada, from foothills to Mount Whitney, the highest point in the contiguous United States. The General Sherman Tree, the largest tree on Earth by volume, grows in its Giant Forest. Bobcats, mule deer and rattlesnakes live in the foothills.
matters: The Giant Forest holds five of the ten largest trees in the world. UNESCO named the area a Biosphere Reserve in 1976.
